svg.title: The six steps of Layer 3 design in fixed order, with the consequence of getting each one wrong
svg.desc: Six numbered steps in a left column with, for each, the decision to be made and the consequence of getting it wrong: addressing plan and summarizability, domain and hierarchy split, protocol selection, path design, convergence and stability, boundaries and redistribution. Step one is emphasised because summarization capability is a product of the addressing plan, not of the protocol. A lower panel lists the four hard rules for the addressing plan: allocate hierarchically, reserve two to three times the growth space, give loopbacks and management addresses their own block, and plan Internet egress and the DMZ separately. A closing note says each step constrains the next, so a mistake in step one is paid for in steps two to six.
svg.text: Six steps, in this order: each one removes options from the ones that follow
The order is the content — doing step 4 before step 1 means designing on top of a mistake
DECISION
IF YOU GET IT WRONG
Addressing plan and summarizability
does every area get a contiguous block?
is the block sized to be summarised by one prefix?
Not summarizable → the table explodes and every later step becomes damage control.
Domain and hierarchy split
how many IGP areas or levels, and where are the edges?
Too large: one big flooding domain. Too small: complex summaries and paths.
Protocol selection
which IGP, and is BGP needed at all?
Wrong choice → the team cannot operate it; every later decision gets blamed on it.
Path design
primary/backup, load sharing, traffic engineering
You draw lots with default tie-breakers and call the result “behaviour”.
Convergence and stability
time budget per stage, flap suppression
Slow recovery, or a network that flaps continuously and never settles.
Boundaries and redistribution
one-way or two-way, what is tagged, what is filtered
Loops, suboptimal paths and metric pollution — the classic fourth-quarter outage.
Why step 1 is first: summarization capability is a product of the addressing plan, not of the protocol.
Four hard rules: allocate hierarchically (core → region → building → floor) · reserve 2–3× growth per region · give loopbacks
and management their own block (ACLs and policies then reference one prefix) · plan Internet egress and the DMZ separately.
